title: First Koszul homology vanishing gives the polynomial associated graded algebra
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $r\geq0$, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in R$. Put $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ and $B=R/I$ [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. Suppose $H_1(K_R(f_1,\ldots,f_r))=0$, where the Koszul complex and its homology are those of [def-weil-pbc-koszul-complex]. Give $B[T_1,\ldots,T_r]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] the grading in which the coefficients have degree zero and every variable has degree one, and give $\operatorname{gr}_I(R)=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}I^n/I^{n+1}$ the $B$-algebra structure of [def-weil-pbc-associated-graded-ring]. Then the canonical graded $B$-algebra homomorphism
$$\theta:B[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\longrightarrow\operatorname{gr}_I(R),\qquad T_j\longmapsto[f_j]_1,$$
which is the identity on $B$ in degree zero, is an isomorphism. Its degree-$n$ map sends $\sum_{|\alpha|=n}\bar a_\alpha T^\alpha$ to $[\sum_{|\alpha|=n}a_\alpha f_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots f_r^{\alpha_r}]_n$. No Noetherian, local, nonzero-ring, or proper-ideal hypothesis is imposed, and the empty sequence is included.

source.place: Tag 062I, lemma-H1-regular-quasi-regular, specialized to M=R; quasi-regularity is written as the canonical polynomial-to-associated-graded isomorphism.

proof.text: Use the associated graded multiplication and quotient action to evaluate the polynomial variables at $[f_j]_1$. This defines the graded $B$-algebra map $\theta$ by the polynomial universal property. Replacing a lift $a_\alpha$ by $a_\alpha+b_\alpha$, $b_\alpha\in I$, changes its degree-$n$ value by an element of $I^{n+1}$, so its formula is well defined. The ideal $I^n$ consists of sums $\sum_{|\alpha|=n}a_\alpha f^\alpha$: expand a product of $n$ sums of multiples of the $f_j$ and collect terms; the reverse inclusion follows because each monomial is such a product. Thus every degree of $\theta$ is surjective. In degree zero it is the identity. It remains to show that $\sum_{|\alpha|=n}a_\alpha f^\alpha\in I^{n+1}$ forces all $a_\alpha\in I$, for $n\geq1$.

source.place: Tag 062I, lemma-H1-regular-quasi-regular, first paragraph; explicit canonical map and degreewise surjectivity.

proof.text: Assume $r\geq1$. Set $u=(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})$. By induction on $n\geq1$, $H_1(K_R(u,f_r^n))=0$: the base $n=1$ is the hypothesis, and the multiplication lemma applied to the tuples $(u,f_r^n)$ and $(u,f_r)$ gives the next exponent. For any tuple $t$, the equality $H_1(K_R(t))=0$ means every relation $\sum c_jt_j=0$ is a boundary $d_2(w)$. Since $d_2(e_i\wedge e_j)=t_ie_j-t_je_i$, every coordinate of that boundary belongs to the ideal generated by $t$. In particular, the last coordinate of every relation for $(u,f_r^n)$ belongs to $(u,f_r^n)\subseteq I$.

source.place: Tags 062G and 062I, lemma-mult-koszul-regular (1) and lemma-H1-regular-quasi-regular, second paragraph.

proof.text: Fix $n\geq1$ and $\xi=\sum_{|\alpha|=n}a_\alpha f^\alpha\in I^{n+1}$. Write $a=a_{(0,\ldots,0,n)}$. Every other degree-$n$ monomial contains some $f_i$ with $i<r$, so $\xi=\sum_{i<r}A_if_i+af_r^n$. Likewise every degree-$(n+1)$ monomial except $f_r^{n+1}$ contains such an $f_i$, so $\xi=\sum_{i<r}B_if_i+bf_r^{n+1}$. Subtracting gives $\sum_{i<r}(A_i-B_i)f_i+(a-bf_r)f_r^n=0$. The preceding boundary-coordinate calculation yields $a-bf_r\in(u,f_r^n)\subseteq I$, hence $a\in I$. This argument is valid over every commutative coefficient ring with the same H1 hypothesis, including $r=1$, where both sums over $i<r$ are empty.

source.place: Tag 062I, lemma-H1-regular-quasi-regular, second paragraph: the pure last-power coefficient.

proof.text: Pass to $S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_{r-1}]$. The low Koszul terms have their explicit exterior bases. A degree-one cycle $z$ for $f$ over $S$ has a finite expansion $z=\sum_\beta x^\beta z_\beta$ with $z_\beta\in R^r$. Because the entries of $d_1$ are the constants $f_i$, the equality $d_1z=0$ says $d_1z_\beta=0$ coefficientwise. For each nonzero coefficient choose $w_\beta\in K_2(R,f)$ with $d_2w_\beta=z_\beta$, using the original $H_1=0$. Then the finite sum $\sum_\beta x^\beta w_\beta$ has boundary $z$. Thus $H_1(K_S(f))=0$ directly, without invoking flatness or descent.

source.place: Tag 062I, lemma-H1-regular-quasi-regular, final paragraph: polynomial extension, checked coefficientwise instead of quoting flat base change.

proof.text: In $S$ put $g_i=f_i-x_if_r$ for $i<r$ and $g_r=f_r$. They generate $IS$, because $f_i=g_i+x_ig_r$. In degree one send the standard vector $e_i$ of the $g$-tuple to $v_i=e_i-x_ie_r$ for $i<r$ and send $e_r$ to $v_r=e_r$ in the $f$-tuple. This is invertible by $e_i\mapsto e_i+x_ie_r$. It intertwines $d_1$ because $d_1^f(v_i)=g_i$. In degree two send $e_i\wedge e_j$ to $v_i\wedge v_j$; expanding the displayed $d_2$ formula gives $d_2^f(v_i\wedge v_j)=g_iv_j-g_jv_i$, the image of $d_2^g(e_i\wedge e_j)$. These two invertible maps take cycles and boundaries bijectively to cycles and boundaries, proving $H_1(K_S(g))=0$.

source.place: Tag 062I, lemma-H1-regular-quasi-regular, final paragraph; Tag 0625, lemma-change-basis, specialized triangular calculation in degrees 0,1,2.

proof.text: Rewrite $\xi$ over $S$ by $f_i=g_i+x_ig_r$ for $i<r$ and $f_r=g_r$. It is a homogeneous degree-$n$ expression in the $g_j$, and the coefficient of $g_r^n$ in that formal expansion is $p(x)=\sum_{|\alpha|=n}a_\alpha x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_{r-1}^{\alpha_{r-1}}$: to get only $g_r$ one must choose $x_ig_r$ from every factor. Since $H_1(K_S(g_1,\ldots,g_r))=0$ by step 5, the induction of step 2 over $S$, with [lem-per-h1-koszul-last-product] applied to the tuples $(g_1,\ldots,g_{r-1},g_r^m)$ and $(g_1,\ldots,g_{r-1},g_r)$, gives $H_1(K_S(g_1,\ldots,g_{r-1},g_r^n))=0$. Since $\xi\in I^{n+1}\subseteq(IS)^{n+1}=(g_1,\ldots,g_r)^{n+1}$, the coefficient argument of step 3 for the tuple $g$ over $S$ gives $p\in IS$. Write $p=\sum_j f_jq_j(x)$. Each coefficient of $p$ is therefore a sum of multiples of the $f_j$, so lies in $I$. Distinct $\alpha$ of total degree $n$ give distinct $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_{r-1})$, because $\alpha_r=n-\sum_{i<r}\alpha_i$. Consequently each coefficient in question is exactly $a_\alpha$, proving all $a_\alpha\in I$. This includes $r=1$, when $S=R$ and $p$ has just one coefficient.

source.place: Tag 062I, lemma-H1-regular-quasi-regular, final paragraph: generic triangular substitution and coefficient extraction. Homogeneity permits using r-1 polynomial variables instead of the source Laurent extension.

proof.text: For a homogeneous degree-$n$ polynomial over $B$ in the kernel of $\theta$, choose coefficient lifts to $R$. Its value lies in $I^{n+1}$; steps 2--6 show that every coefficient lift is in $I$, so the original polynomial is zero. Degree zero was already the identity. A general polynomial is the finite sum of its homogeneous parts, and distinct graded summands cannot cancel, so $\theta$ is injective. Together with step 1 it is bijective; its inverse preserves the $B$-algebra operations and grading by applying injectivity to their images. If $r=0$, then $I=0$, both algebras are $R$ concentrated in degree zero, and $\theta$ is the identity. If $I=R$ (including the zero ring), $B=0$ and all $I^n/I^{n+1}$ vanish, so both algebras are zero. No properness or finiteness assumption has been used.
